articles.title: Shortcuts to the good bit

body.support:
Handbooks and manuals are long. Nobody reads every page. Use the **shortcuts**.

**The front**

- **Blurb:** the short bit on the back. What's the book about?
- **Contents page:** the chapters and their page numbers.

**The middle**

- **Headings:** titles for each part. Jump to the one you need.
- **Bold words, boxes and tables:** the important bits.

**The back**

- **Index:** an A to Z list of topics and pages.
- **Glossary:** what the tricky words mean.

**Pick a keyword.** What word are you looking for? Not there? Try another word that means the same.

**Skim or scan?**

- **Skim** for the main idea. Read the headings.
- **Scan** for one fact. Look for your keyword.

**Tricky words.** Break them up. *Un-road-worthy* = not good enough for the road.
body.core:
Handbooks, manuals, course guides and rule books are long. Nobody reads them from page one to the end. Smart readers use **shortcuts**.

**The front**

- **Cover and blurb:** the title, and a short description on the back. They tell you what the book is about and who it's for.
- **Contents page:** the chapters, in order, with the page each one starts on. Use it when you want a whole topic, like *“Buying a car”*.

**The middle**

- **Headings and subheadings:** titles for each section. They let you jump straight to the right part.
- **Bold words, boxes, tables and pictures:** these usually show the most important information.

**The back**

- **Index:** an A to Z list of topics, with every page they appear on. Use it when you want one specific thing, like *“tyres”* or *“towing”*.
- **Glossary:** a mini-dictionary of the tricky words in the book.

**Pick your keyword.** Before you look, decide what word you're searching for. If it's not in the index, try another word that means the same thing. *“P plates”* might be listed under *“probationary licence”*.

**Skim or scan?**

- **Skim** when you want the main idea. Read the headings, the first line of each paragraph, and anything in bold.
- **Scan** when you want one fact. Run your eyes down the page looking for your keyword or a number. Stop when you find it, then read that part carefully.

**Tricky words.** Break them into parts you know. *Unroadworthy* = *un* (not) + *road* + *worthy* (good enough): not good enough for the road. Words come in families: *licence*, *licensed*, *licensing*.
body.extend:
Reference texts such as handbooks, manuals, course guides and policy documents are designed to be navigated, not read sequentially. Efficient readers use their navigational features.

**Front matter**

- **Cover and blurb:** identify the text's topic and intended audience.
- **Contents page:** lists chapters and sections in order, with starting pages. Best for locating a broad topic.

**Body**

- **Headings and subheadings** signal each section's content, so you can move directly to what's relevant.
- **Visual emphasis** (bold type, boxes, tables, diagrams) usually flags key information.

**Back matter**

- **Index:** an alphabetical list of specific topics with every page reference. Best for locating a precise detail.
- **Glossary:** definitions of specialised terms.

**Keywords and synonyms.** Decide on a **keyword** before searching. If it isn't listed, try synonyms or related terms (*“P plates”* may appear under *“probationary licence”*).

**Skimming and scanning.** **Skim** for gist: headings, topic sentences, emphasised text. **Scan** for a specific item: move your eyes rapidly in search of a keyword or number, then read the surrounding text closely.

**Decoding unfamiliar words.** Use morphology and word families. *Unroadworthy* breaks into *un-* (not), *road* and *worthy* (fit for). Related forms (*licence*, *licensed*, *licensing*) share meaning.

caseStudies.title: One book, 32 questions

body.support:
In Victoria, you need to pass a **test** to get your Ls.

The test has **32 questions**. You need 25 right to pass.

All the questions come from one book: **Road to Solo Driving**. You need to know all four chapters.

That's a lot! But the book has shortcuts: a contents page, headings, boxes and pictures.

VicRoads has a free **practice test** online. If you get one wrong, it tells you which chapter to look in.

So: do the practice test. Find the chapter. Use the headings. Scan for the answer.
body.core:
In Victoria, before you can get your learner permit (your Ls), you have to pass a **knowledge test**.

The test has **32 questions**, picked at random. To pass, you need **78%**: that's 25 or more correct.

All the questions come from one book: **Road to Solo Driving**, the official handbook. VicRoads says the questions are based on **all four chapters**, so you need to know the whole book.

That sounds like a lot. But Road to Solo Driving is built to be searched, not just read. It has a contents page, chapters with clear headings, and lots of boxes, tables and pictures.

VicRoads also has a free **practice test** online. It's similar to the real one. When you get a question wrong, it points you to the **chapter** in the handbook where the answer is.

So the smart way to study is to use the shortcuts. Do a practice test. Find the chapter for each question you got wrong. Use the headings to find the right section. Scan for the answer, then read it carefully.

It's the same skill you'll use with any manual, rule book or course guide for the rest of your life.
body.extend:
In Victoria, applicants for a learner permit must pass a **knowledge test**.

The test has **32 questions**, randomly generated, and a pass mark of **78%** (at least 25 correct).

Every question is drawn from **Road to Solo Driving**, the official handbook. VicRoads advises studying the whole book, because questions come from **all four chapters**.

That's a substantial text. But it's designed to be navigated: a contents page, chaptered sections with clear headings, and information organised in boxes, tables and diagrams.

VicRoads also offers a free online **practice test** that mirrors the real one. Incorrect answers link to the handbook **chapter** that covers the topic.

The efficient study strategy is therefore navigational. Attempt a practice test, use the chapter references and headings to locate each topic, scan for the specific rule, then read that section closely.

The same approach applies to any manual, policy, rule book or course guide you'll meet at work or in training.

model.text:
**Book:** Road to Solo Driving

**My question:** How far away from a fire hydrant do I have to park?

**How I found it**
1. I looked in the **index** at the back, under P for “parking”.
2. The index sent me to the parking pages.
3. I used the **headings** to find “Where you must not park”.
4. I looked down the list for the word “hydrant”.

**Time:** About 40 seconds.

**What I learned:** For one small fact, the index is faster than the contents page.

teacher.overview: Students learn to navigate informative and instructional texts using the cover and blurb, contents page, headings, emphasised text, index and glossary; to choose between skimming (main idea) and scanning (a specific fact); to try synonyms when a keyword isn't listed; and to decode unfamiliar words using word parts and word families. They annotate a handbook's features, sort where to look, decide skim or scan, and race to find answers in a real handbook. The case study is Victoria's learner permit knowledge test: 32 random questions with a 78% pass mark, all drawn from the four chapters of Road to Solo Driving, with a free practice test that points to the relevant chapter.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** contents lists chapters at the front (for whole topics); index lists specific topics A to Z at the back (for details). Skim for the main idea; scan for one fact. Try a word that means the same thing.

**Handbook:** 1 blurb; 2 contents page; 3 headings; 4 box with key info; 5 index; 6 glossary.

**Sort:** insurance chapter — contents; towing — index; roadworthy certificate — glossary; how it's set out — contents; tyre tread — index; third-party property — glossary.

**Skim or scan:** night driving main idea — skim, headings and first lines; phone number — scan for numbers; right manual — skim the cover, blurb and contents; P1 passengers — scan the index for “passengers” or “P1”.

**Case study:** wrong answers point to the chapter, so you know where to look; questions come from all four chapters; contents, headings, index, boxes.

realityCheck: **Many students want their Ls.** The case study is genuinely useful; let them try the practice test.
**Online handbooks have search.** Talk about when Ctrl+F helps and when the contents or headings work better.
**Bring real books.** Manuals and cookbooks make the race more fun than worksheets.
**Works in a real class:** yes. A quick win that builds confidence with long texts.
